concept.name: Binomial distribution
concept.definition: The discrete probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials, each with exactly two outcomes and the same success probability p. It is the sum of n independent Bernoulli variables and is probably the most commonly used discrete distribution.
concept.intuition: It answers: 'If each trade wins with probability p, what are the chances of exactly x wins in n trades?' The win count, not the order of wins, is what matters.
concept.mechanics: The probability of x successes equals the number of ways to choose which x trials succeed (the binomial coefficient) times p^x(1-p)^(n-x). It requires a fixed number of trials, two outcomes per trial, constant p, and independence; the maximum likelihood estimate of p from data is x/n.
concept.formula: P(X = x) = C(n,x) * p^x * (1-p)^(n-x) for x = 0..n, where C(n,x) = n!/(x!(n-x)!); mean = np, variance = np(1-p).
concept.failure_modes: The independence and constant-p assumptions fail under regime changes, serial correlation, or sampling without replacement, in which case binomial probabilities misstate tail odds. For large n and small p it is better approximated by the Poisson distribution, and for large n with moderate p by the normal.
concept.misconceptions: The binomial counts successes without regard to order or payoff size - it cannot price P&L, only event counts. And 'more wins than expected' over n trades is not proof of skill; with p = 0.5, 12+ wins in 20 trials still occurs about 25% of the time.
concept.example: A strategy wins with p = 0.55 per trade; the probability of exactly 15 wins in 20 trades is C(20,15) * 0.55^15 * 0.45^5, about 0.037.
